The films exhibit low surface roughness and high purity, with nickel content exceeding 97%.
evidence: We report the growth of nickel metal films by atomic layer deposition (ALD) employing bis(1,4-di-tert-butyl-1,3-diazadienyl)nickel and tert-butylamine as the precursors. Saturation plots demonstrated self-limited growth for both precursors, with a growth rate of 0.60 Å/cycle. The nickel metal ALD process demonstrates inherent selectivity for metal substrates for at least 1000 cycles at 180 °C.

We recently proposed that treatment of physisorbed 2 with tert-butylamine would lead to the formation of a 5-coordinate adduct, in which the tert-butylamine nitrogen atom coordinates to the cobalt(II) ion in 2. This coordination would distort the tetrahedral geometry, possibly to square pyramidal, and significant energy changes in the d orbitals would occur. Such coordination would lower the decomposition temperature of surface-bound 2, thus giving cobalt metal at lower temperatures than pure 2. Complexes 1 and 2 contain metal(II) ions bonded to radical anion ligands. Thermal decomposition of 1 likely occurs by formation of the 5-coordinate adduct 3, followed by transfer of the electrons from the ligands to the metal ion, thus affording nickel metal.

This study explores the atomic layer deposition (ALD) of indium oxide (In2O3) films using cyclopentadienyl indium (InCp) and combinations of both molecular oxygen and water as the co-reactants. When either O2 or H2O were used individually as the oxygen source, the In2O3 growth was negligible over the temperature range 100–250 °C. However, when oxygen and water were used in combination either as a simultaneous exposure or supplied sequentially, In2O3 films were deposited at growth rates of 1.0–1.6 Å/cycle over the full range of deposition temperatures. In situ quadrupole mass spectrometry and quartz crystal microbalance measurements revealed that water serves the function of releasing ligands from the surface while oxygen performs the role of oxidizing the indium. Since both processes are necessary for sustained growth, both O2 and H2O are required for the In2O3 ALD.

value: The study investigates the reaction chemistry during the atomic layer deposition (ALD) of Sc2O3 and Gd2O3 using Sc(MeCp)3, Gd(iPrCp)3, and H2O. evidence: The reaction chemistry during the ALD of Sc2O3 and Gd2O3 from Sc(MeCp)3, Gd(iPrCp)3, and H2O was investigated by in situ time-resolved quadrupole mass spectrometry. The remaining ligands were then removed by hydrolysis during the H2O pulse. The films are deposited using alternating pulses of tetrakis-ethylmethylamino hafnium and H2O precursors at 250 °C. The nucleation process on H-terminated surfaces initially shows a barrier, which is overcome after the 7th cycle. The interfacial layer formed on H-terminated surfaces is detected and remains stable. A comparison of the nucleation stage of the films on OH- and H-terminated Si surfaces has been performed using Rutherford backscattering spectrometry, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and spectroscopic ellipsometry. We find for the initial 5–7 process cycles that the film nucleates more efficiently on the OH-terminated surface. However, after the 7th cycle both surfaces exhibit similar surface coverage, which takes about 40 cycles to reach a steady growth rate per cycle. Angle resolved XPS measurements reveal the formation of a 6 Å interfacial layer after four ALD cycles on the H-terminated surface and the thickness of the interfacial layer does not change substantially between the 4th and the 50th process cycles as shown by transmission electron microscopy. Atomic force microscopy measurements reveal higher surface roughness for the films deposited in the H-terminated surface. The SE and the AFM data are consistent with higher porosity for the films on H-terminated surfaces.

We studied and optimised the properties of ultrathin superconducting niobium nitride films fabricated with a plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD) process. By adjusting process parameters, the chemical embedding of undesired oxygen into the films were minimised and a film structure consisting of mainly polycrystalline niobium nitride with a small fraction of amorphous niobium oxide and niobium oxo-nitrides were formed. For this composition a critical temperature of 13.8 K and critical current densities of 7x10^6 A/cm² at 4.2 K were measured on 40 nm thick films. A fundamental correlation between these superconducting properties and the crystal lattice size of the cubic δ-niobium-nitride grains were found. Moreover, the film thickness variation between 40 and 2 nm exhibits a pronounced change of the electrical conductivity at room temperature and reveals a superconductor-insulator-transition in the vicinity of 3 nm film thickness at low temperatures.

The ALD process consists of a set of sequential, self-limiting deposition processes that operate on the principle of alternating saturating surface reactions. During ALD, a substrate is exposed to a precursor vapor that forms a monolayer or sub-monolayer of the precursor on the surface of the substrate. High-quality Pt thin films are prepared by atomic layer deposition (ALD) using metal-organic precursors dimethyl-(N,N-dimethyl-3-butene-1amine-N) platinum (C8H19NPt) and with diluted molecular oxygen (O2) as a reactant. The films are grown at a relatively low temperature of 225 °C on a thermally grown SiO2 substrate, and the process shows all the necessary qualities of an ideal ALD such as self-limiting growth characteristics and a well-defined ALD temperature window between 200 and 250 °C. Noticeably, the current ALD-Pt process shows a very high growth per cycle of 0.167 nm without an incubation period at 225 °C, and perfect conformality is obtained at a dual trench structure (top and bottom width: 40 and 15 nm) with an aspect ratio of around 6.3. The resistivity of the ALD-Pt film at ∼39 nm in thickness deposited at 225 °C is almost the same (∼10.8 μΩ cm) as its bulk resistivity (10.6 μΩ cm), and it is as low as ∼12 μΩ cm at 25 nm in thickness.

Deposition of thin and conformal copper films has been examined using atomic layer deposition as possible seed layers for subsequent electrodeposition. The Cu films were deposited on glass plates as well as on Ta, TiN, and TaN films on silicon wafers. The Cu precursor for our current investigation was copper(II)-1,1,1,5,5,5-hexafluoroacetylacetonate hydrate or Cu(hfac)2·XH2O. The Cu films were deposited on 50 x 50 mm substrates that included glass plates and silicon wafers that were precoated with a 500 nm layer of SiO2, followed by an ~6 nm thick barrier layer. A typical ALD cycle consisted of a 12 s Cu(hfac)2 pulse, then a 20 s N2 purge, followed by a 12 s reducing agent pulse, and finally another 20 s N2 purge. The Cu source was heated to 75°C and the reducing agents were all at room temperature. Although deposition of Cu was observed in all cases at ~230°C, the results reported here were produced at 300°C, unless otherwise noted.

This paper reports on recent results of silicon molecular layer epitaxy (MLE) using SiH2C12 and hydrogen. Growth conditions for monomolecular layers by the monomolecular layer deposition process have been investigated as a function of substrate temperature, pressure in the growth chamber, gas injection time, and vacuum evacuation time. The substrate temperature of 825~ was best suited to the monomolecular layer growth where the film thickness per cycle is saturated with the SiH2C12 injection pressure. From the results obtained by mass spectrometry and IR spectroscopy, we may conclude that in the MLE growth the most predominant surface-adsorbed migrating species on silicon is SIC12. Also, the autodoping profiles of boron and other impurities have been measured by SIMS.

value: The paper presents a kinetic model to predict the conformality of atomic layer deposition (ALD) by considering the effect of sticking probability on film thickness profiles. The model was validated using experimental data from the TMA/H2O ALD process in macroscopic test structures.
evidence: The conformal deposition of ultrathin films is important in many technologies. In microelectronics, the continuous miniaturization of electronic devices poses strong requirements for the deposition techniques used in integrated circuit manufacturing. Good conformality has become an important requirement, because ultrathin films need to be grown in trenches and holes with increasing aspect ratios. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is known as an excellent technique for conformal coating. ALD can be defined as a cyclic process which relies on sequential self-terminating reactions between gas-phase precursor molecules and a solid surface. The self-terminating nature of the chemical reactions ensures precise film-thickness control and excellent step coverage. To achieve full coverage of high-aspect-ratio features, it is of crucial importance that process parameters are optimized. To this end, several experimental and theoretical studies have been done to understand ALD into high-aspect-ratio structures. Elam et al. studied Al2O3 and ZnO in ultrahigh-aspect-ratio nanopores of anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) membranes. The conformality depended on the precursor pulse time, and for too short pulses only the parts of the nanopores near the open ends were fully covered. The ZnO coverage profiles showed that the film thickness decreased as a function of depth in the pores. Recently, Perez et al. developed a transmission electron microscopy methodology to quantify the conformality of ALD of HfO2 in AAO nanopores. These measurements also revealed a slope of decreasing thickness in the coverage profiles. Gordon et al. suggested a kinetic model describing the diffusion and deposition inside holes. In this model, a sticking probability of 100% was assumed for precursor molecules hitting an uncovered section of the wall of the hole, while molecules hitting a fully covered section had zero probability to stick. This assumption resulted in a stepwise film-thickness profile after a single ALD cycle. However, the experimental studies mentioned above, as well as our own experimental results described later in this article, indicate a gradual decrease of film thickness instead of the stepwise drop as envisioned by Gordon et al. It has been argued that the gradual slope typically observed in experimental thickness profiles may be related to the increasing aspect ratio during deposition or the sticking probability, which is less than 100%. The first explanation seems reasonable for the case of microscopic trenches, because during each cycle the deposition of new material results in a decrease of the diameter of the hole, and consequently the effective aspect ratio increases during deposition. However, experiments using macroscopic test structures also show a gradual decrease, suggesting that the sticking probability is an important parameter for predicting the conformality of ALD growth. In this paper, an extension is proposed to the model suggested by Gordon et al., where the sticking probability is now related to the surface coverage by Langmuir’s equation s(θ) = s0(1−θ). Therefore, the initial sticking probability for zero coverage s0 can be treated as an adjustable model parameter. To validate the model, experiments were performed to quantify the conformality for the trimethylaluminum (TMA)/H2O ALD process using macroscopic test structures.

The self-limiting growth has been shown to occur through the following reaction process, as shown in Fig. 1. At first, for the ALE-AlAs growth, the decomposed Al-containing molecules start to adsorb onto the As-stabilized surface (Fig. 1a). Al atoms are incorporated into the Al sites of AlAs, and alkylradicals that are connected to the Al atoms then terminate the Al-stabilized surface. Once the alkylradical-terminated Al surface is formed, further adsorption of Al-containing materials does not occur. Growth proceeds until the surface is fully covered by Al atoms with alkyl radicals. In the next hydrogen purge step (Fig. 1b), alkyl radicals start to desorb from the surface, and a bare Al metal surface appears. Next, sufficient AsH3 gas is supplied to the surface (Fig. 1c), and this gas reacts with Al atoms to form AlAs. Finally, hydrogen is purged to completely remove extra As atoms (Fig. 1d).

Ultrathin tin oxide films were deposited on flat hotplate templates using atomic layer deposition (ALD) techniques with SnCl4 and H2O2 as the reactants. A wide range of SnOx ALD film thicknesses between 15.9 Å and 58.7 Å was prepared by varying the number of sequential, self-limiting SnCl4 and H2O2 reactions. The CO gas sensor response increased for increasing thicknesses between 15.9 Å and 26.2 Å and decreased for increasing thicknesses between 26.2 Å and 58.7 Å.
